# 4 Maccabees Chapter 11 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** The Mother's Speech and Deaths

---

**1** The most admirable mother embraced each of her sons in turn as they were brought out and said to them in the language of their fathers: My son, have pity on me who carried you nine months in the womb and nursed you for three years.

**2** I urge you, my child, to look at the sky and the earth and to consider all the things in them, and to know that God made them all out of nothing.

**3** And so it is that the creator of mankind also created you; and if you turn your heart toward him and receive his comfort, you will live.

**4** I am not afraid of this tyrant; and I will willingly share in your sufferings, in hopes that I may shame this tyrant of our world.

**5** I am your father and your mother, your nurse and the guide of your youth, and your instructor in wisdom; and I urge you: do not be afraid, for you did not come into the world without the will of God.

**6** Think upon all this and do not be discouraged, for it is for the sake of the law that you are dying.

**7** She was still saying these words while the guards led her away to her death.

**8** O most wretched of all tyrants! Most barbarous of all! Does not your heart break when you see how they look at you?

**9** Does not pity seize you when you behold this aged mother of seven children being treated in this way?

**10** And yet she bears all this joyfully for the love of God.

**11** She is truly a mother of virtue, for it is God who has implanted virtue in souls.

**12** Now indeed, O tyrant, you have unjustly put to death these seven brothers.

**13** But you have not enslaved their reason, and you have not conquered their virtue.

**14** Rather, it is you who have been conquered — conquered by reason! You who rule over all these peoples have been overcome by an aged woman and her seven sons.

**15** The noble mother of the seven, having herself witnessed the deaths of all seven of her sons, and having honored them by encouraging them all to a noble death, ended her own life in the same noble manner.

**16** She kept her spirit as though she were going to a great festival, glorying in God, so that nothing could break her resolve.

**17** Let this narrative be sufficient proof that devotion to reason masters even the worst suffering.

**18** For if a woman, and she an aged woman, with seven young men was able to overcome the tyrant, it is plain that devotion to God is master of the passions.

**19** I have shown this to be true not only in the case of the wise men I have named, but I have also demonstrated it through the story of the seven brothers and their mother.

**20** All of them together have proved the sovereignty of reason over the passions.

**21** Therefore it is fitting that I call them blessed — Eleazar and the seven brothers and their mother.

**22** For having endured all their sufferings and torments and burnings, they have been victorious. The holy ones now reign; they are at rest with their ancestor Abraham. Not one of them failed or wavered.

**23** Not one of the brothers said, Would that I had not been brought here! Not one of them said, Would that I had eaten the defiling food!

**24** Not one of them turned back; not one shrank from death. Not one was robbed of the reward of valor. From the first to the last, they each maintained their fidelity.
